name: Hair micropigmentation

card.summary: A scalp tattoo that mimics a buzz cut or camouflages scars; long-lasting, but backed by press coverage rather than studies.
card.note: Hairline placement matters; removal requires laser.

quick.overview:
Scalp micropigmentation tattoos tiny dots onto the scalp to look like shaved hair follicles. People use it for baldness, thinning density or to hide scars.

It typically takes several sessions and is described as permanent, though touch-ups and laser removal are possible.
quick.mechanism: Pigment is placed in the superficial skin, matched to existing hair colour, to imitate the shadow of cropped hair.
quick.risks: Allergic reaction to ink is a stated concern, and a poor hairline can look unnatural. No peer-reviewed studies were identified.

lead: Hair micropigmentation, usually called scalp micropigmentation (SMP) or a hair tattoo, is a non-surgical cosmetic tattoo applied to the scalp. It creates the look of a closely shaved head on a bald scalp, adds apparent density to a thinning crown or part line, and camouflages hair-transplant scars and other scalp scars.[1][2]

Wikipedia describes the procedure as typically taking three to four sessions of about two hours each, with pigment matched to the colour of the client's existing hair, and as long lasting but removable by laser.[1] A 2013 review in Facial Plastic Surgery Clinics describes it as labour-intensive, sometimes requiring multiple sessions and up to 20 hours of procedure time.[3]

Dermatology reviews present SMP as a camouflage option alongside medication and transplantation, particularly where conditions such as cicatricial alopecia leave few other choices.[4][5] A 2015 review reports very high patient satisfaction in the author's series.[2]

chain: Pigment dots are placed in the superficial scalp
They read as cropped hair follicles
Bald or thin areas look like a shaved head with density
angle.text: The tattooed dots imitate the shadow of short hair, so a bald or thinning scalp looks like a closely buzzed head. People also use it to blend a hair-transplant scar or to make a thinning part look denser.

infobox: Three to four of about two hours[1]
Described as permanent; laser removal possible[1]
Simulated buzz cut, density, scar camouflage[1][2]

paras: The technique deposits pigment in the superficial skin in a stippling pattern, using cosmetic tattoo instruments and pigments, to imitate hair follicles.[2] Practitioners may perform a small patch test first for ink allergy, and the hairline is described as the most important part of the work, with a poorly executed hairline looking unnatural. The hairline can reportedly be adjusted or touched up over time.[1]

On trichoscopy, SMP appears as evenly spaced, homogenous grey to black round dots that are larger than adjacent hair follicles, a finding that has been correlated with histopathology in a case report.[6]

A review of the technique lists a range of alopecias that are hard to treat and hair-transplant deformities as conditions SMP can conceal.[2] A 2022 review states SMP is now considered a major means of hair-loss management alongside medication and transplantation, and covers the practical principles for natural-looking results.[7] A hair camouflage review in the International Journal of Trichology includes SMP among options from hairpieces to permanent methods.[4]

A 2024 retrospective study of 40 women with female pattern hair loss who had undergone both hair transplantation and SMP examined factors, including measured hair density and caliber, that might guide choosing between them.[8]
Coverage of celebrity scalp tattoos appeared in The Hollywood Reporter in 2013, and ABC News and Men's Health ran pros-and-cons pieces in 2012 and 2013 respectively.[1]

Published work is mostly narrative reviews, technique descriptions and small series. The 2015 review reports high patient satisfaction and discusses tattoo-pigment histology and regulation,[2] the 2013 review covers technical considerations,[3] and a 2024 comparative study reviewed 40 female patients treated with both transplantation and SMP.[8] No large randomized trials were identified.
A 2022 case report correlated trichoscopic and histologic features of SMP.[6]

Wikipedia states allergic reactions are a concern that patch testing aims to address, and that no long-term side-effect data have been reported over the past decade with reputable ink, a statement flagged as needing a citation.[1] The 2013 review notes the skin of each patient holds the dye differently, so the technique is customized and sometimes needs several sessions.[3]

On looksmax.org, a thread comparing SMP with a hair system has one member saying SMP helps mainly for people who always wear a bald look, have gaps after a transplant, or have diffuse thinning, and that hair systems are the better option for typical male pattern baldness; another adds that a skull shape suited to a buzz cut matters.[9]

timeline.event: ABC News publishes a pros-and-cons piece on scalp tattoos.[1]
Facial Plastic Surgery Clinics review describes SMP as a treatment for balding or thinning hair.[3]
Review in the Journal of Clinical and Aesthetic Dermatology describes SMP as a concealer for hair and scalp deformities.[2]
Review of techniques for natural-looking SMP results is published.[7]

lore.intro: In looksmaxxing forums SMP is discussed as a buzzed-look option and is compared with hair systems and transplants.[9]

claims.claim: SMP only suits certain hair situations
claims.believers: One looksmax.org poster says it works for people who always keep a bald look, have missing hairs after a transplant or have diffuse thinning, and a second adds that the wearer needs a skull shape that suits a buzz cut.[9]
claims.experts: Reviews describe SMP as a camouflage for alopecias and transplant deformities, with natural results depending on technique and patient factors.[2][7]

claims.claim: Hair systems look better than SMP for male pattern baldness
claims.believers: The same poster calls hair systems superior for typical male pattern baldness.[9]
claims.experts: No published study compares SMP with hair systems; a 2024 study compared SMP with transplantation in women.[8]
